entry.title: W T H Pty Ltd v Fair Work Ombudsman [2026] FCA 1650
entry.content:
The Federal Court determined whether the Vehicle Manufacturing, Repair, Services and Retail Award 2010 and the Vehicle Repair, Services and Retail Award 2020 applied to car hire employees working as vehicle service agents and rovers, rather than the General Retail Industry Award. Justice Raper found the employees' cleaning, detailing, servicing and triaging duties fell within the Vehicle Awards' classifications (including car cleaner/washer), and that the Vehicle Awards applied to the exclusion of other modern awards.

entry.title: Income Asset Management Group Limited v Henry (No 2) [2026] FCA 1642
entry.content:

Mr Henry sought his costs of defending the discontinued claim. entry.title: Application by Communications, Electrical, Electronic, Energy, Information, Postal, Plumbing and Allied Services Union of Australia (128V) [2026] FWC 4267
entry.content:
In [2026] FWC 4267, the CEPU applied under s 437 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for a protected action ballot order covering employees of Country Club Tasmania. The employer initially objected on genuineness, prematurity and ballot-question clarity grounds but did not press those objections at the hearing. Deputy President Wright was satisfied the statutory requirements were met and made the order.

Key holding: Under s 437(3)(b), ballot questions comply if they are capable of yes/no answers and propose action of an identified character capable of constituting industrial action under s 19(1), without a separate informed-consent requirement.

In summary, therefore, an application for a protected action ballot order will comply with the requirement in 437(3)(b), and thus will have been "made under section 437" for the purpose of s 443(1)(a), if it specifies a question or questions, capable of being answered "yes" or "no" by the employees participating in the ballot, which propose(s) action of an identified character, kind or sort capable of constituting industrial action within the meaning of s 19(1).

entry.title: Mr Davide Tamburella v The Trustee For La Costa Hospitality Unit Trust [2026] FWC 4264
entry.content:
Mr Tamburella lodged a s 365 general protections dismissal application 28 days after the 21-day statutory deadline. The Fair Work Commission refused an extension of time because it was not satisfied that exceptional circumstances existed. The application was dismissed.

Key holding: Exceptional circumstances under s 366(2) require assessment of all the circumstances and must be out of the ordinary course, unusual, special or uncommon, though need not be unique or unprecedented.

In summary, the expression 'exceptional circumstances' has its ordinary meaning and requires consideration of all the circumstances. To be exceptional, circumstances must be out of the ordinary course, or unusual, or special, or uncommon but need not be unique, or unprecedented, or very rare.

entry.title: Ms Rosmiaty Tarigan v Respect Group Limited [2026] FWC 4273
entry.content:
This case concerns an application by Ms Rosmiaty Tarigan under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy against Respect Group Ltd. The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application because Ms Tarigan repeatedly failed to comply with directions and did not prosecute her case. The decision was made on the Commission’s own initiative under s.587.

Key holding: The Fair Work Commission may dismiss an unfair dismissal application on its own initiative under s.587 where an applicant’s unreasonable and repeated failure to comply with directions means they have not put their case and the claim has no reasonable prospects of success.

For these reasons, I consider that it is appropriate to dismiss Ms Tarigan's application on the basis that having failed to put her case before the Commission, her claim has no reasonable prospects of success. Pursuant to s.587, the Applicant's unfair dismissal application is dismissed.

entry.title: Matthew Allan Doyle v Secure Journeys Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4272
entry.content:
Matthew Allan Doyle made an unfair dismissal application under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 after his dismissal took effect on 28 April 2026; the application was lodged on 16 September 2026, 120 days outside the 21-day period. The Fair Work Commission refused an extension of time because it was not satisfied there were exceptional circumstances under s 394(3).

Key holding: An extension of time under s 394(2)(a) requires the Commission to be satisfied of exceptional circumstances under s 394(3), which is a high hurdle not met where the explanation for delay is unacceptable and the other factors are neutral or against an extension.

The test of exceptional circumstances in s 394(3) of the Act establishes a high hurdle for an applicant for an extension of time.

entry.title: Mr Cameron McLary v Bold Electrical Group Pty Ltd & Mr Neal Radford [2026] FWC 4268
entry.content:
Mr McLary lodged a s.365 general protections (dismissal) application one day outside the 21-day statutory period, having been dismissed effective 26 May 2026 and filing on 17 June 2026. He sought an extension of time, belatedly arguing that his dismissal actually took effect on 1 June 2026 because termination/leave payments were processed to that date. The Commission rejected that argument and, finding no exceptional circumstances, declined to extend time and dismissed the application.

Key holding: An applicant seeking an extension of time under s.366(2) bears the onus of adducing evidence establishing exceptional circumstances; a late-asserted, unsubstantiated dismissal date will not supply that explanation.

An applicant for an extension of time has an onus to adduce evidence in support of matters which that applicant asserts constitute exceptional circumstances.

entry.title: Thomas Strang v Wesfarmers Kleenheat Gas Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4260
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission dismissed Mr Strang’s s 365 dismissal application because it was lodged outside the 21-day statutory timeframe and he did not respond to the Commission’s directions about seeking an extension of time. The application was dismissed on the Commission’s own initiative for want of prosecution under s 587(3)(a) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).

Key holding: The Commission may dismiss an application on its own initiative for want of prosecution where the applicant’s conduct or omissions show they are no longer willing to participate in their case, provided procedural fairness has been afforded.

Section 587 of the Act allows the Commission to dismiss an application if it is apparent that an applicant has stopped pursuing or participating in the proceedings that they commenced. Section 587(3)(a) allows the Commission to dismiss an application on its own initiative, so long as the applicant has been afforded procedural fairness.

entry.title: Kaur v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1651
entry.content:
The applicant sought leave to appeal from a decision of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Div 2) refusing an extension of time to review a Registrar's summary dismissal of her judicial review application. The underlying Tribunal decision affirmed refusal of a Regional Employer Nomination (subclass 187) visa because her employer's nomination had not been approved. Hill J dismissed the leave application and fixed costs at $5,000.

Key holding: Where a subclass 187 visa criterion requires an approved employer nomination, and the nomination has never been approved and can never now be approved, refusal is the only decision open and leave to appeal will be refused because remittal would be futile.

In this case, as explained, the Tribunal made the only decision that was open to it to make: the Applicant's employer nomination was not approved at the time of the Tribunal's decision, and therefore the 187 visa could not be granted. Further, the Tribunal has refused an application to review the refusal of that employer nomination.

entry.title: Miss Patricia Smith v Luke Reynolds Hairdressing Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4251
entry.content:
The Fair Work Commission determined a jurisdictional objection to Patricia Smith’s unfair dismissal claim against Luke Reynolds Hairdressing Pty Ltd. The employer had 13 employees after excluding the owner/director and an externally engaged bookkeeper, so it was a small business employer and the one-year minimum employment period applied. Because Ms Smith had worked for less than one year, her application was dismissed: Smith v Luke Reynolds Hairdressing Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4251.

Key holding: Where an employer is a small business employer under s 23, the minimum employment period is one year under s 383(b), and an employee with shorter service is jurisdictionally barred from an unfair dismissal claim.

If the Respondent is a small business employer and the 1-year period applies, the application will be jurisdictionally barred. If the Respondent is not a small business employer, the 6 month period will apply and the application will continue.

entry.title: Mr Rayto Mark v Thrive House Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4254
entry.content:
This was an unfair dismissal application by Mr Rayto Mark against Thrive House Pty Ltd. The Commission upheld the employer’s jurisdictional objection that Mr Mark had not completed the six-month minimum employment period, because his employment relationship commenced on his first client-facing shift on 4 December 2025, not when he signed the contract or undertook paid induction/training. The s.394 application was dismissed.

Key holding: Where an employment contract makes commencement conditional on completing screening and pre-employment requirements and identifies the first client-facing shift as the commencement point, the employment relationship and s.384(1) period of employment commence at that first shift, notwithstanding earlier paid induction or training.

For the above reasons , taking into consideration the case law and the evidence and submissions from the parties, the first shift undertaken by the Applicant (on 4 December 2025), commenced the employment relationship between the parties; this is when the Applicant 's period of employment commenced pursuant to s.384(1) of the Ac t. This commencement date is set out to occur in this manner in the employment contract .

entry.title: Mr Christopher Prasser v Tailored Designs Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 4256
entry.content:
The Applicant lodged an unfair dismissal application under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) against a non-small-business employer. The Respondent objected on jurisdiction, contending the Applicant had served less than the six-month minimum employment period. The Commission determined the employment relationship commenced on 12 January 2026 and the dismissal took effect on 10 July 2026, so the application was jurisdictionally barred and dismissed.

Key holding: The period of employment for the minimum employment period is measured from when the employment relationship commences, which may be later than the date the contract of employment is formed.

In this matter, the contract of employment came into existence on 9 January 2026, however the employment relationship did not come into existence until 12 January 2026 as was stipulated as the commencement date in the offer signed by the Applicant and when the Applicant commenced work for the Respondent.

entry.title: Application by Macmahon Underground Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1997
entry.content:

The Commission found Macmahon had obtained acceptable alternative FIFO Truck Operator roles at other sites, despite no written offers, and reduced the redundancy pay to nil.

Key holding: A role may be “obtained” under s 120(1)(b)(i) without a formal written offer where the evidence shows the employee was told the role was available and it was offered informally.

However, the evidence of numerous conversations with Ms Robb in which the roles were satisfies me that she was aware the roles were available to her and that they had been offered in an informal sense. Particularly, the conversation on 10 March 2026 in my view evidences that the Applicant had offered to return Ms Robb to a Truck Operator role and the consequences of not accepting a Truck Operator role would be a redundancy.

entry.title: Cheng v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1631
entry.content:
The Federal Court dismissed Ms Cheng’s judicial review application challenging an Administrative Review Tribunal decision that affirmed non-revocation of her visa cancellation under s 501(3A). The Court rejected claims that the Tribunal committed jurisdictional error in its treatment of her drug history, rehabilitation evidence, community expectations and legal consequences. The application was dismissed with costs.

Key holding: HZCP prevents a Tribunal from going behind facts that support the conviction and sentence, but it does not bar consideration of historical facts that did not support the sentence.

So, even if the finding by the sentencing judge is to be construed as a finding that Ms Cheng had never been a drug user, it was only the finding as at the time of offending that supported the sentencing. The principles in HZCP did not concern factual findings that did not support the sentence that was made.

entry.title: Singh v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1638
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a dismissal of judicial review of a Tribunal decision refusing a partner visa because the appellant did not satisfy Schedule 3 criterion 3001 and the Tribunal was not satisfied there were compelling reasons to waive it. The appellant raised numerous grounds, including new points and late AI-prepared grounds, but the Court refused leave for most new points and dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: In migration appeals, leave to raise a new point not taken below may be granted where it clearly has merit and there is no real prejudice to the respondent, but is generally refused where there is no adequate explanation and the point is of doubtful merit.

Specifically in relation to migration cases, where an adverse decision may have various serious consequences for an appellant, the Court may grant leave to raise such a new point that was not taken below if the point clearly has merit and there is no real prejudice to the respondent in permitting it to be agitated.

entry.content:
